title: Dynamic Programming
relevance: DP is a core OA/interview topic for recognizing overlapping subproblems, designing states/recurrences, and optimizing space on classic patterns (knapsack, LCS, stocks, LIS, partition/MCM).

phases.goal: Establish when DP applies and the four-step pedagogy from recursion through space optimization.

must_hit.point: DP applies when a problem has overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names both overlapping subproblems (same subproblem recomputed) and optimal substructure (optimal answer from optimal sub-answers).

must_hit.point: Naive recursive Fibonacci is exponential: time O(2^n) because identical subproblems like F(n-2) are recomputed many times.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States F(n)=F(n-1)+F(n-2) and cites O(2^n) from the recomputation tree.

must_hit.point: Memoization caches recursive results to O(n) time; tabulation builds iteratively from base cases; if only a constant number of prior states are needed, the O(n) table can shrink to O(1).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Walks the ladder: top-down cache → bottom-up table → keep only the few predecessors (e.g. F(n-1), F(n-2)).

must_hit.point: Heuristic signals for DP: try-all-choices / min-max / number-of-ways plus a state that repeats during exploration.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions those problem phrasings together with repeated state during search.

probes: When is a problem a DP problem, and how do you go from a recursive Fibonacci solution to an O(1)-space solution?

hints.1: Think about what makes recomputation wasteful and what properties let you reuse answers.
hints.2: Walk the four-step ladder: recursion → memoization → tabulation → space optimization.
hints.3: Say overlapping subproblems + optimal substructure; naive F is O(2^n); memo/tabulation O(n); Fibonacci space-opts to O(1) with two variables.

phases.goal: Check that the candidate can design states and recurrences for the main DP templates in the material.

must_hit.point: State-design recipe: express f(index, …), write the recurrence to subproblem states, then identify base cases.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists the three recipe steps in order.

must_hit.point: Climbing stairs / 1D path: f(i)=f(i-1)+f(i-2) with base f(1)=1, f(2)=2; frog-with-K uses min over j in 1..K and costs O(n × k) time.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives the stairs recurrence and bases, and the K-jump min over prior K steps with O(n × k).

must_hit.point: Pick/not-pick on a 1D sequence: house robber f(i)=max(f(i-1), f(i-2)+arr[i]); circular House Robber II solves two linear ranges excluding first or last.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States pick vs not-pick and the circle reduction to max of two linear robber passes.

must_hit.point: Subsequence/knapsack state is usually (index, target/weight); take OR not-take for subset sum; unbounded take stays at the same index.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names index+constraint state, boolean take|notTake for subset sum, and stay-on-index for unbounded coins/knapsack.

must_hit.point: String DP compares prefixes f(i,j): LCS match → 1+f(i-1,j-1), mismatch → max(f(i-1,j), f(i,j-1)); Edit Distance mismatch tries insert/delete/replace each costing 1.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives LCS match/mismatch transitions and the three edit ops with +1.

must_hit.point: Partition/MCM: state is a range [i,j], try every partition k; MCM cost adds arr[i-1]*arr[k]*arr[j]; Burst Balloons picks the last balloon in the range so subranges become independent.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes range DP, the MCM multiply cost formula, and last-to-burst reasoning for balloons.

probes: Write the recurrence and base cases for House Robber, then for 0/1 Knapsack versus unbounded coin change, then for LCS.

hints.1: Start from choices at the current index or cell, then name what else the state must remember.
hints.2: For sequences use pick/not-pick or index+target; for strings compare prefixes; for MCM try every cut k in [i,j].
hints.3: Robber: max(skip i, take i + f(i-2)); knapsack take uses index-1, unbounded take stays at index; LCS match 1+diag else max(up,left).

phases.goal: Probe space/time tradeoffs and the 1D knapsack loop-direction rule grounded in which row the recurrence reads.

must_hit.point: When the current row only needs the previous row (grids, LCS, subset-sum rows), a full 2D table can collapse to one or two 1D arrays; many 1D path DPs further collapse to two variables / O(1).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains previous-row rolling arrays and the two-variable optimization when only i-1 and i-2 matter.

must_hit.point: Frog Jump with K cannot easily reduce to O(1) variables; need O(n) (or at least size K) for tabulation.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts K-jump needing an array of size O(n) or K versus two-variable classic frog.

must_hit.point: 1D knapsack dual-identity: 0/1 must iterate weight backward so reads stay on the previous row; unbounded iterates forward so reads chain on the current row.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States golden rule: 0/1 backward preserves past; unbounded forward chains present, tied to which row the recurrence names.

must_hit.point: LIS can be O(n^2) DP over previous indices, or O(n log n) via a temp tails array and lower_bound (temp length is LIS length, not necessarily a valid LIS).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts nested prev-loop DP with binary-search tails / lower_bound caveat.

probes: Why does 0/1 Knapsack’s 1D array go right-to-left while Unbounded goes left-to-right? What breaks if you swap them?

hints.1: Ask what value still sits in dp[w] before versus after you overwrite it this row.
hints.2: 0/1 recurrence reads previous index/row; unbounded take reads same index at smaller weight.
hints.3: Backward keeps yesterday’s cells so each item is used once; forward reuses today’s updates (infinite supply). Wrong direction silently solves the other problem.

phases.goal: Apply patterns to reductions, multi-agent states, reconstruction, and common interview pitfalls.

must_hit.point: Partition Equal Subset Sum: odd total sum is impossible; even sum reduces to subset sum of total_sum/2. Target Sum / partitions-with-difference reduce to counting subsets with sum (total_sum ± D or target)/2 when that quantity is valid.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the odd-sum reject and the algebraic reduction to one subset-sum/count instance.

must_hit.point: Cherry Pickup II: both robots share one state f(i,j1,j2) with 3×3=9 move pairs; running one robot then the other misses overlapping decisions.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Bundles both columns into one state and cites nine transitions / same-row movement.

must_hit.point: Count subsets with zeros: picking or not picking a zero changes the subset but not the sum; if arr[0]==0 and target 0, base ways are 2.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains zero doubles ways and the index-0 base of 2 when the first element is 0.

must_hit.point: Interview flow: recognize try-all-ways + overlapping states, name a template, state the recurrence f(i,j)=… before coding, then discuss space-optimizing when the current row depends only on the previous.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Echoes the interview checklist: pattern → recurrence spoken aloud → optional rolling-array space talk.

probes: How would you reduce Target Sum to a known DP, and how would you model two robots collecting cherries on the same grid?

hints.1: For signed sums, think positive vs negative subsets; for two agents, ask what must be known at the same time.
hints.2: Derive S1=(total+target)/2 for Target Sum; for cherries keep row i and both columns.
hints.3: Target Sum → count subsets of (total_sum+target)/2 (if even/feasible); Cherry Pickup II → f(i,j1,j2) with nine child transitions, not two separate passes.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Memoization caches recursive calls and keeps recursion-stack overhead while pruning the tree to linear states for Fibonacci-style problems; tabulation drops recursion, fills from base cases upward, and more clearly exposes which prior cells are needed for space cuts.

tradeoffs.topic: Full DP table vs rolling / O(1) space
tradeoffs.strong_answer: If state i only needs i-1 and i-2 (stairs, classic frog, house robber), the O(n) array becomes two variables / O(1). Grid/LCS/subset-sum rows that only need the previous row collapse to O(min dimension) or O(k) 1D arrays. Dependencies on K prior steps or on many interval lengths (MCM) block aggressive O(1) collapse.

After crushing dp[index][w] to dp[w], a cell is ‘yesterday’ before overwrite and ‘today’ after. 0/1 must read the previous row → iterate w from W downward. Unbounded’s take stays on the same index → iterate upward so w-weight already includes this item. On the file’s example weights {2,4,6}, values {5,11,13}, W=10: forward yields 27 (unbounded), backward yields 24 (0/1).

tradeoffs.topic: O(n^2) LIS DP vs O(n log n) patience/tails
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Classic DP tries all previous indices for O(n^2) time and can reconstruct via a parent/hash array. The tails array + lower_bound runs in O(n log n) for length only; the temp array is not necessarily a valid LIS.

gotchas.trap: Implementing 0/1 Knapsack with a left-to-right 1D loop (or Unbounded right-to-left).
gotchas.correction: Wrong direction silently becomes the other variant: forward 0/1 overcounts (too large); backward unbounded undercounts (too small). Neither crashes; samples where each item is taken once can hide the bug.

gotchas.trap: Ignoring zeros when counting subsets with sum K.
gotchas.correction: A zero does not change the sum but doubles subset choices; if the first element is 0, prev[0] must be 2 (take or leave), not 1.

gotchas.trap: Assuming an odd-sum array can be partitioned into two equal-sum subsets.
gotchas.correction: If total_sum is odd, equal integer halves are impossible; only even totals reduce to subset sum of total_sum/2.

gotchas.trap: Solving Cherry Pickup by running one robot to completion then the other.
gotchas.correction: Concurrent actors need one unified state (row + both columns); sequential passes miss jointly optimal overlapping cell choices (same cell counted once).

gotchas.trap: Bursting balloons by choosing which to burst first in a range.
gotchas.correction: First-burst order couples neighbors so subproblems are not independent; choose the last balloon k in [i,j] so neighbors are nums[i-1] and nums[j+1] and the sides separate.

gotchas.trap: Returning front-partition palindrome-cut DP without subtracting the implicit final cut.
gotchas.correction: The recurrence adds a cut after every palindrome piece including the end; return f(0)-1 so a fully palindromic string correctly costs 0 cuts.

gotchas.trap: Treating Longest Common Substring like LCS on mismatch.
gotchas.correction: On mismatch, contiguous common suffix length resets to 0; track a global max over the table rather than only dp[n][m].

gotchas.trap: Assuming the O(n log n) LIS temp array is the actual subsequence.
gotchas.correction: Replacements keep smallest tails for each length; only temp.size() is the LIS length—reconstruction still needs the O(n^2) parent-pointer method.
